show: Szeretve mind a vérpadig, the Hungarian historical musical by Medveczky–Pécsváradi–Vizeli after Jókai Mór's novel, performed by Magyarock Dalszínház
synopsis:
Tisza Ilonka waits for a marriage arranged by her mother, Tisza Istvánné Zsuzsanna, while the household prepares for celebration. Before the wedding can bind her future, disaster enters the house: her brother, Tisza Gábor, has been killed in a duel, and the bridegroom is then brought home dead after a labanc attack on the wedding party. Ilonka’s grief is sharpened by the knowledge that the marriage was never her own choice, and the ruined ceremony leaves the family exposed as the country moves toward rebellion.

In the Rákóczi-szabadságharc, Ocskay László rises at the side of II. Rákóczi Ferenc. A daring officer, he wins battles and takes fortresses, becoming the feared and celebrated “Rákóczi villáma.” Around him gather commanders and rivals: Bercsényi Miklós directs the Hungarian forces, Vak Bottyán changes sides to serve the Hungarian cause, while Pálffy János and Heister lead the opposing imperial armies. Ocskay’s private life becomes inseparable from the war. His marriage to Tisza Ilonka offers the possibility of devotion and belonging, but Szunyoghy Ozmonda’s presence and the pull of ambition deepen his uncertainty.

Victories, loyalties, and personal attachments begin to fray under the strain of a prolonged conflict. Ocskay, brilliant in action but unable to settle his inward conflict, drifts from the cause that made him famous. Intrigue surrounds him, and men such as Sárody Vencel profit from betrayal and divided allegiance. The hero once hailed for striking the enemy becomes a figure suspected and condemned by his own side. His reversal culminates in capture and execution at Érsekújvár, while those who loved him must confront the distance between the man they knew and the traitor history remembers.

The musical turns war into a test of identity: public duty clashes with private love, and heroism can corrode into isolation. Its central tragedy lies in the cost of wavering loyalty—and in the enduring love that remains even when a man is led to the scaffold.

show: Egri csillagok – A nagy musical, the Hungarian musical by Várkonyi Mátyás and Béres Attila after Gárdonyi Géza's novel, performed by Magyarock Dalszínház and Paulay Ede Színház
synopsis:
Bornemissza Gergely and Cecey Éva are seized as children by the one-eyed Jumurdzsák as invading Turkish forces ravage Hungary. Bound for sale as slaves, the children escape their captor and take his talisman with them—a loss that leaves the superstitious Jumurdzsák convinced that fortune has turned against him. Their flight forges an enduring bond between Gergely and Éva, while it also begins Jumurdzsák’s relentless desire for revenge.

Years pass, and the conflict reaches Eger. Turkish armies surround the fortress, whose defence is entrusted to Dobó István. Gergely returns as a resourceful fighter, reunited with Éva amid the escalating danger, while their private history with Jumurdzsák resurfaces inside the larger struggle for survival. The defenders must confront not only overwhelming military force but also the corrosive danger of betrayal, fear, tempting promises, and divided loyalties. Dobó holds his people to a severe standard of commitment: the fortress cannot be surrendered, and he pledges to share every hardship demanded of those who stand with him.

Under Dobó’s leadership, the men and women of Eger turn determination, ingenuity, and mutual loyalty into resistance. Gergely’s courage is bound both to his love for Éva and to the fate of the fortress, while Jumurdzsák’s pursuit gives the siege a personal, vengeful edge. As the encirclement tightens, the defenders endure a near-impossible contest whose outcome becomes a defining victory rather than a mere escape from defeat.

The musical centres on steadfastness under pressure: love and personal loyalty are tested within a collective fight to protect home and freedom. It contrasts courage and ingenuity with treachery, coercion, and vengeance, presenting Eger’s defence as a victory won through shared resolve.

show: Valahol Európában, the Hungarian musical in two acts by Dés László, Nemes István, Böhm György, Korcsmáros György and Horváth Péter, staged at the Magyar Színház in Budapest
synopsis:
Somewhere in a Europe torn apart by war, hungry, homeless children have learned to survive in a roaming band rather than expect mercy from adults. Hosszú helps lead the group with hard-won authority, while Suhanc—Éva—guards a painful secret and distrusts men. Alongside Ficsúr, Szeplős, Sutyi, Csóró, Suttyó, Professzor, Pötyi, and the other children, they steal food, evade pursuers, and cling to one another as their only remaining family.

Seeking somewhere safe to sleep, the band reaches a ruined castle inhabited by Simon Péter, an elderly musician and conductor. To children who have been brutalised by war, an adult is automatically an enemy; Simon is at first treated as a threat and nearly hanged. Yet he does not answer their fear with violence. Gradually, through patience, warmth, and the transforming force of music, he earns a place among them. The castle becomes more than shelter: it becomes a space in which the children can begin to recover trust, play, sing, and imagine a life not governed solely by hunger and danger.

That fragile refuge is tested when the children are found out and adults from the surrounding country set out to seize them, closing in on the castle. Simon and the band choose not to abandon one another. They defend their home together, and in the shooting one of the youngest, Kuksi, is fatally wounded — to save him the band must carry him down into the village, knowing that capture is certain. Kuksi does not survive, but Simon returns from the town with an order clearing the children of the thefts hunger had forced on them and handing the castle over into their own possession, giving permanence to the belonging they had created together.

The musical centres on children reclaiming dignity after loss, and on the difficult choice to trust again when the world has taught them fear. Its enduring themes are solidarity, courage, freedom, friendship, and the humanising power of love and music.

show: Ezeregy éjszaka, the Hungarian musical staged at the Magyar Színház in Budapest
synopsis:
Seherezádé is led before King Sahriár, a ruler hardened by betrayal into murderous distrust: after his wife’s infidelity, he has resolved to take a new bride each night and have her killed by morning. A captive herself, Seherezádé stays alive by beginning a tale whose ending she withholds until the next dawn. Night after night, her storytelling opens portals into crowded bazaars, glittering palaces, desert roads and enchanted realms, while the king—initially cold and impatient—finds himself compelled to hear what comes next.

Within these tales, Harún, a young ruler stripped of his throne and of his sight, is swept into dangers far beyond anything the court had prepared him for. His path crosses that of Ali(da), a resourceful thief whose wit turns the powerful’s assumptions against them, and Jázmin, the beautiful princess whose fate is entangled with the ambitions of others. Their adventures bring them up against Dzsáfár, whose schemes threaten love, freedom and the balance of the kingdom. The talkative Dzsinn, freed from his bottle, offers marvels and wishes, but magic never removes the need for courage or good judgement; encounters with Maszrúr, an ifrit, a fortune-teller and even a tree that grows human heads test the travellers at every turn.

As Seherezádé prolongs each cliff-hanger, the stories do more than delay her sentence. Their thieves, princes, monsters and lovers expose the consequences of greed, cruelty and blind authority, and they repeatedly make room for loyalty, ingenuity and mercy. King Sahriár gradually moves from listening merely for diversion to confronting the wound that has governed his rule. By the time the separate adventures accumulate into a sustained emotional reckoning, Seherezádé’s voice has become a force capable of challenging his fear and restoring his capacity to trust.

The musical centres on the redemptive power of storytelling: imagination becomes both Seherezádé’s means of survival and King Sahriár’s path back to empathy. It also celebrates courage, love and quick wits as answers to tyranny, vengeance and despair.
